lead: This unit explains the network under a mobile app: how a phone stays connected while its user moves. You will learn the cellular system from GSM to 5G, frequency reuse, handover and Mobile IP, then Wi-Fi, Bluetooth and ad hoc networks. After it you can read a mobile network diagram, size a cell cluster and trace a packet to a moving device.
about: The unit moves from the big picture to the network layer. Chapter 1.1 defines mobile computing and its three parts: device, wireless link and fixed network. Chapter 1.2 puts the generations in order, from analog voice to 5G data. Chapter 1.3 opens up GSM, GPRS and UMTS, the systems behind 2G and 3G. Chapter 1.4 explains why an operator can reuse the same frequency in distant cells, and how channels are allotted. Chapter 1.5 follows a moving user: handover keeps the call alive, and location areas keep the network's records current. Chapter 1.6 carries IP packets to a moving node with Mobile IP. Chapter 1.7 covers Wi-Fi and Bluetooth, the short-range links inside buildings, and 1.8 ends with ad hoc networks that need no base station at all.

chapters.idea: Mobile computing is computing done by a user who is moving, and it always has three parts: a device, a wireless link, and a fixed network with middleware.
chapters.depth: Definition first: a mobile host changes its point of attachment while a session runs. Cover the usual characteristics (ubiquity, location independence, adaptivity, personalisation, connectivity, small battery-powered device), the three-part structure (mobile host, wireless access network, fixed network plus middleware for location, security and sync), and four application areas with Indian examples: UPI payments, IRCTC ticketing, telemedicine, fleet tracking. Only a few universities teach this chapter; keep it to the structure and its vocabulary, with one clean example per part.

figure.title: Structure of a mobile computing system
figure.aria: A five-box chain from a phone, over a radio link and mobile middleware, into the fixed network and a server.

chapters.example: A UPI app on a phone sends a 2 KB request. The 4G link runs at 5 Mbps and the one-way delay is 40 ms. Find the time to push the request onto the link, and the total one-way time. 2 KB = 2048 bytes = 16 384 bits. Transmission time = 16 384 ÷ 5 000 000 = 3.3 ms. Total = 3.3 + 40 = 43.3 ms. The delay dominates, not the data rate.
chapters.trap: Treating mobile and wireless as the same thing. A laptop carried on a train with no radio is mobile but not wireless; a desktop on Wi-Fi is wireless but not mobile.
chapters.leave: Android app anatomy and tools go to Unit 2; mobile security and app publishing go to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Each cellular generation added one new capability, from analog voice to all-IP data.
chapters.depth: Order the generations by what each added: 1G analog voice (AMPS, NMT), 2G digital voice and SMS (GSM, IS-95 cdmaOne), 2.5G packet data (GPRS, EDGE), 3G (UMTS/WCDMA, CDMA2000), 3.5G (HSDPA), 4G (LTE, all-IP, OFDMA), 5G (NR, mmWave, network slicing). Give one data rate per generation as an order of magnitude only. Close with one line each on satellite systems and terrestrial broadcast systems as other delivery paths to a mobile user. Do not teach internal architecture here.

figure.aria: A timeline of five cellular generations, each bar showing the commercial era of its main standard from AMPS to 5G NR.

chapters.example: A 5 MB song is about 40 Mbit. Find the download time on 2G at 9.6 kbps, on 3G at 384 kbps, and on 4G at 20 Mbps. 2G: 40 000 000 ÷ 9600 = 4167 s, about 69.4 min. 3G: 40 000 000 ÷ 384 000 = 104.2 s, about 1.7 min. 4G: 40 000 000 ÷ 20 000 000 = 2 s.
chapters.trap: Calling GPRS a 3G system, or assuming every higher number means a brand-new air interface: 2.5G and 3.5G are upgrades inside the same system.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for the device, link and network picture.
chapters.leave: GSM, GPRS and UMTS internals go to Chapter 1.3; cell planning goes to 1.4.

chapters.idea: GSM carries voice over circuits, GPRS adds packet data to the same network, and UMTS replaces the radio with WCDMA.
chapters.depth: GSM: the mobile station (ME plus SIM), the base station subsystem (BTS and BSC) and the network subsystem (MSC, VLR, HLR, AUC, EIR). Name the interfaces Um, Abis and A. Radio side: 200 kHz carriers, 8 time slots per 4.615 ms frame, FDMA plus TDMA. GPRS: SGSN, GGSN, PDP context, attach, always-on packet data. UMTS: UTRAN made of Node B and RNC, WCDMA on 5 MHz carriers, soft handover. Keep one comparison line for circuit versus packet.

figure.title: GSM network and the GPRS/UMTS additions
figure.aria: A downward chain from the mobile station through the base station and controller to the switch, with the home register attached to the switch and a link to the outside network.

chapters.example: A GSM cell has 4 carriers. Each carrier has 8 time slots in a 4.615 ms frame, so a slot lasts 4.615 ÷ 8 = 577 µs. One slot carries the control channel. How many calls can run at once, and what is the frame rate? Calls = 4 × 8 − 1 = 31 traffic channels. Frame rate = 1 ÷ 4.615 ms = 216.7 frames per second.
chapters.trap: Swapping HLR with VLR, or SGSN with GGSN. HLR is the permanent home record; VLR is the temporary copy for the visited area. SGSN routes packets to the mobile; GGSN is the gateway to the Internet.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.2 for where 2G and 3G sit in the timeline.
chapters.leave: Handover signalling and location updates go to Chapter 1.5; IP delivery over the packet core goes to 1.6.

chapters.idea: A cellular operator can reuse the same frequencies in cells far enough apart that interference stays tolerable.
chapters.depth: Hexagonal layout and the cluster. Cluster size N = i² + ij + j² for shift integers i and j. Reuse distance D = R√(3N) with cell radius R. Co-channel ratio Q = D/R = √(3N). Signal-to-interference for six co-channel interferers and path-loss exponent k: SIR = Q^k ÷ 6; with k = 4 this is 1.5 N². Channel allocation: fixed, dynamic and hybrid, plus borrowing. Mention Erlang-B capacity in one line only. Only a few universities teach the Erlang and CDMA capacity comparison; keep it to a sentence.

figure.aria: A centre cell A ringed by six neighbouring cells B to G, each holding a different frequency group in a seven-cell cluster.

chapters.example: Take i = 2 and j = 1. Then N = 4 + 2 + 1 = 7. With cell radius R = 1 km, reuse distance D = 1 × √21 = 4.58 km. With path-loss exponent k = 4, SIR = (√21)⁴ ÷ 6 = 441 ÷ 6 = 73.5, that is 10 log₁₀ 73.5 = 18.66 dB. If the operator owns 350 channels, each cell gets 350 ÷ 7 = 50 channels.
chapters.trap: Using D = R√N instead of R√(3N), and forgetting the six interferers in the denominator of the SIR formula.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.3 for what a cell and a carrier are.
chapters.leave: Handover between the cells goes to Chapter 1.5; Erlang tables and CDMA capacity comparison are one-line mentions only.

chapters.idea: Mobility management has two jobs: handover keeps a call alive as the user moves, and location tracking lets the network find an idle user.
chapters.depth: Handover types: hard (break before make) and soft (make before break, WCDMA only). The four phases: measurement, initiation, decision, execution. Show the main messages between MS, old BSS, new BSS and MSC, and the VLR update when the MSC changes. Location management: location area, attach and detach, location update, paging, HLR and VLR records. One line on SDN and NFV in cellular network management: centralised control and virtualised core functions. Keep signalling to the main messages only.

figure.aria: A message sequence in which the mobile measures, the switch sets up the new base station, the mobile switches over, and the old channel is released.

chapters.example: A call lasts 120 s and the user crosses a cell boundary every 15 s. Each hard handover breaks the link for 60 ms. Handovers = 120 ÷ 15 = 8. Total break = 8 × 60 ms = 480 ms. Fraction of the call lost = 0.48 ÷ 120 = 0.4 percent.
chapters.trap: Saying the phone sends a location update at every cell change. It updates when it enters a new location area; inside the area the network pages the phone.
chapters.prereq: Chapters 1.3 and 1.4 for the GSM databases and for cell boundaries.
chapters.leave: Registration and tunnelling across the Internet go to Chapter 1.6; SDN and NFV get one line here, no depth.

chapters.idea: Mobile IP lets a node keep one permanent address while it attaches to foreign networks, using a home agent and a tunnel.
chapters.depth: Entities: mobile node, home agent, foreign agent, correspondent node. Agent discovery (agent advertisement and solicitation), registration with the home agent, care-of address, IP-in-IP tunnelling, decapsulation at the foreign agent. Triangle routing and route optimisation. MIPv6 with binding updates and no foreign agent. Only a few universities teach this chapter; cover tunnelling and the triangle route, then stop. One line on SDN and NFV in the cellular core is enough.

figure.title: Mobile IP: packet path through the home agent
figure.aria: A packet from the correspondent goes to the home agent, is tunnelled to the foreign agent, and reaches the mobile node, with a dashed direct route also shown.

chapters.example: A correspondent sends a 100-byte payload. The original IP header is 20 bytes, so the datagram is 120 bytes. IP-in-IP tunnelling adds a 20-byte outer header, so 140 bytes cross the tunnel. Overhead = 20 ÷ 120 = 16.7 percent. On a 2 Mbps link the tunneled datagram takes 1120 ÷ 2 000 000 = 0.56 ms.
chapters.trap: Confusing the home address, which never changes, with the care-of address, which is temporary and belongs to the visited network.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.5 for mobility inside one operator; this chapter extends mobility across networks.
chapters.leave: Wireless link behaviour and error modelling get one line each; the full transport-layer study over wireless channels is beyond this book.

chapters.idea: IEEE 802.11 shares a radio channel politely with CSMA/CA, while Bluetooth builds small piconets around one master.
chapters.depth: 802.11 architecture: station, access point, basic service set, extended service set, distribution system. Protocol architecture: PHY and MAC layers. MAC management frames: beacon, probe, authentication, association. Channel access: CSMA/CA with DIFS, SIFS and backoff, RTS/CTS, the hidden node problem. Bluetooth: piconet with one master and up to seven active slaves, scatternet, FHSS over 79 channels, time-division duplex, link manager and profiles, physical and MAC layers. Name HIPERLAN/2 and WATM in one line as rival broadband wireless systems. Only a few universities teach this chapter; keep both systems at architecture level.

figure.title: 802.11 extended service set
figure.aria: Two basic service sets, each with an access point, joined by a distribution system backbone.

chapters.example: An 802.11b network sends 1500-byte data frames at 11 Mbps. Frame bits = 1500 × 8 = 12 000. Transmission time = 12 000 ÷ 11 000 000 = 1.09 ms. Preamble, ACK, DIFS and backoff add about 0.50 ms. Efficiency = 1.09 ÷ 1.59 = 68.6 percent.
chapters.trap: Saying Wi-Fi uses CSMA/CD like Ethernet. A radio cannot listen while it transmits, so 802.11 uses collision avoidance, and adds RTS/CTS for hidden nodes.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for the access-network part of the mobile system.
chapters.leave: HIPERLAN/2, WATM, satellite and broadcast systems are named only; ad hoc routing goes to Chapter 1.8.

chapters.idea: A mobile ad hoc network is a set of nodes that route for each other with no base station and no fixed backbone.
chapters.depth: Characteristics: no infrastructure, multi-hop paths, topology that changes with every move, limited energy, limited bandwidth. Applications: disaster relief, vehicle networks, sensor fields, tactical use. Routing classes: proactive table-driven (DSDV), reactive on-demand (AODV, DSR), hybrid (ZRP). Explain route request flooding, route reply, route error, and the broadcast storm problem. One line on TCP performance over ad hoc paths. Only a few universities teach this chapter; stop at route discovery.

figure.aria: Five nodes where the route from source A runs through B to destination D in two hops, with side links to C and E.

chapters.example: Source A has neighbours B and C. B is a neighbour of D; C is a neighbour of E. A wants a route to D. A broadcasts one route request. B and C each rebroadcast it once, so 3 broadcast transmissions cross the network. D answers B by unicast, and B forwards the reply to A. Route found: A to B to D, which is 2 hops.
chapters.trap: Assuming a MANET needs an access point, or that a route stays valid for the whole session. Routes expire and are rebuilt when nodes move.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.7 for the radio link, the hidden node problem and CSMA/CA.
chapters.leave: TCP behaviour over multi-hop paths and MANET security get one line each.

links: the three parts of a mobile system explain what each generation improved
2G and 3G in the timeline are opened up as GSM, GPRS and UMTS
GSM cells need spectrum, so the same frequencies are reused
cells meet at boundaries, where handover takes over
mobility inside one operator is extended across the Internet
packet delivery ends at a short-range wireless link
Wi-Fi with an access point becomes a network with none
